extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, translators, and students of imaginative literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, translating, and judging works of pure imagination (poems, romances, visionary/prose narratives), with emphasis on language, imagery, moralizing, originality, and re-readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obtruding the moral sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: In works of pure imagination the obtrusion of a moral sentiment openly on the reader is a fault; a poem or tale should not present its moral as the operative cause of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: The Ancient Mariner's chief fault is 'the obtrusion of the moral sentiment so openly on the reader as a principle or cause of action in a work of such pure imagination.' Prefer subtlety: allow moral feeling to emerge without explicit didactic imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use very plain language for imaginative works
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of imagination should be written in very plain language; the more purely imaginative they are the more necessary it is to be plain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Plainness preserves the realism/credibility of visionary material. Anti-pattern: over-ornamented or elevated diction in highly imaginative pieces can alienate readers or break the imaginative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not polish away the realism of visionary writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive polishing or refining of the language in a visionary work can destroy the reality of the vision it conveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Pilgrim's Progress 'is composed in the lowest style of English... If you were to polish it, you would at once destroy the reality of the vision.' Preserve plain, unvarnished expressions where they serve the imaginative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve primary visual images in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating (e.g., the Psalms), preserving the primary visual images often better preserves connection and force of sentences than over-interpretive or paraphrastic renderings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: favor literal or image-faithful renderings of key nouns/visuals. Example: 'If the primary visual images had been oftener preserved, the connection and force of the sentences would have been better perceived.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal rendering of primary sense can illuminate text
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering the bare primary sense (literally) of original terms can throw additional light on the text and reveal force lost by paraphrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Coleridge's practice of ascertaining the 'exact visual image or first radical meaning of every noun substantive' in the Psalms; in many cases literal primary sense aids understanding more than an elaborate prophetic/allusive gloss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke feeling to prompt sound thought
rubrics_metrics.description: To move a skeptical or merely intellectual reader toward genuine reasoned conviction, first make them feel — emotional experience (e.g., love) commonly brings a person to a sense of something real, which then enables sound thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: in persuasive or character-driven writing, create sincere emotional stakes to catalyze intellectual or moral change. Anti-pattern: relying solely on abstract argument to change a character's or reader's convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on improbability as a fault
rubrics_metrics.description: Improbability in a tale is not necessarily the chief defect; moral obtrusion can be a greater fault even where probability is questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mrs. Barbauld's criticism that the Ancient Mariner was 'improbable, and had no moral' — the author counters that improbability may be tolerable, but glaring didacticism is the more serious error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer unified, original conception over compositional pastiche
rubrics_metrics.description: A work or character that is 'one and single in projection' and presents an absolutely new idea has a different (often superior) quality than characters constructed by fusing old particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: Undine (presenting an original unified idea) versus Scott (whose best characters are 'composed' from older particulars). Aspiring writers should aim for singular imaginative projections where appropriate rather than mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constant pursuit of prodigious or sensational effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not view nature or description only through the lens of the prodigious or spectacular; cultivate the imagination's capacity to apprehend the true idea of the Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: Martin 'is never satisfied with any appearance that is not prodigious' — writers should temper appetite for grandiosity and train the imagination to perceive subtler beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use register and imagery appropriate to the speaker/subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary imagery and tone with the speaker or subject: ordinary speakers use local/material imagery, while exalted or 'divine' speech should employ loftier, more majestic images to signal difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In the Book of Job, the men's speeches use Eastern/material images, whereas when God speaks the imagery is exalted (Egyptian images like the crocodile, war-horse). Apply register shifts to clarify voice and status in narrative or dramatic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write plainly but avoid slang or false grammar when realism is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain language is valuable for imaginative works, but 'plain' should not lapse into slang or incorrect grammar; plainness supports reality without sacrificing clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Pilgrim's Progress is praised for being 'in the lowest style of English, without slang or false grammar.' Aim for simplicity that preserves diction appropriate to the work's vision and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for multi-layered works that reward re-reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Enduring imaginative works can be read repeatedly at different times with new and different pleasures; they supply material for varied interpretive modes (theological, devotional, poetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design works with depth and polyvalence so they yield new insights across readings and across readers' changing perspectives; avoid one-note, single-purpose tales when longevity and richness are desired.
